newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq's dinar soars, prices plunge on oil deal.
newsitem.headline: Iraq's dinar soars, prices plunge on oil deal.

text.p: Iraqis, hard-hit by U.N. sanctions, rushed to dump dollars at exchange houses on Wednesday as the dinar currency continued to soar following agreement with the U.N. on an oil-for-food deal.
The greenback, which two days ago was worth about 1,650 dinars, was sold for 700 on Wednesday.
"It is the first time since the Hisar (sanctions) people now seriously think keeping dinars could prove to be better than gold or dollars," said a money changer in Baghdad.
Several money changers said they were reluctant to buy dollars despite the dramatic drop in price against the dinar.
Prices of essential commodities also slumped. A tray of 30 eggs dropped to 1,800 dinars from 2,250 on Monday and 3,250 early in the week. A kg (2.2 lb) of cooking oil fell to 900 from about 2,000.

Iraq on Monday agreed to all U.N. terms allowing partial oil sales of $2 billion every six months. Iraq will have access to about $1.2 billion, after paying 30 per cent of the money to 1991 Gulf War victims and about 10 per cent more to cover other U.N. costs.
Iraq's economy has been stifled by U.N. sanctions imposed after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait which led to the war.The oil sales are to allow Baghdad to buy badly needed food and medical supplies.
This is the second time this year news on partial oil sales sent the dinar soaring and prices tumbling in Baghdad.
In January, when Iraq agreed to talks with the United Nations on its oil-for-food offer the dinar soared as high as 450 to the dollar from about 3,000.
The government said on Wednesday it was determined to continue with anti-inflationary measures.

Trade Minister Mohammed Mehdi Saleh, in newspaper remarks on Wednesday, said the government would vigorously pursue its implementation of the economic guidelines laid down by President Saddam Hussein early this year.
Saddam ordered a freeze on money printing and asked ministries to raise money by selling public property and demanding an economic price for their utilities.
Before the latest slash in prices and the surge in local currency Iraqi markets suffered from lack of liquidity. Even state banks complained of the squeeze in money supply.
Iraqis with dinars preferred to lend them to private traders or businessmen rather than depositing them in banks whose interest rate of 10 per cent did not match rampant inflation.
To deter Iraqis from lending to private traders the government vowed on Sunday to punish what it described as "usurers" lending money at excessivly high rates.
Private traders were said to pay up to 20 per cent interest per month.
